title: Simula and the First Classes and Objects (1960s Norway)
explainer: Before 'object-oriented' was a term, Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard at the Norwegian Computing Center built Simula, a language for writing simulations, and its 1967 version (Simula 67) brought together classes, objects, inheritance, and dynamic object creation as a coherent set of ideas for essentially the first time. The ACM later gave Dahl and Nygaard the Turing Award for this work, crediting them as the originators of the object-oriented approach that most modern languages still build on.

title: Alan Kay, Smalltalk, and Coining 'Object-Oriented'
explainer: The phrase 'object-oriented programming' itself was coined by Alan Kay, who led the design of Smalltalk at Xerox PARC in the early 1970s, building on ideas he had seen in Simula. Kay later said he regretted how much attention the word 'objects' drew, arguing that the deeper idea he intended was 'messaging' between independent components — a reminder that the terminology you're learning was one person's specific naming choice, not an inevitable or self-evident one.
